summary.title: C Compiler, Part 10: Global Variables
summary.one_liner: You learn how to add global variables to a C compiler, covering the data and BSS/common sections, variable-map labels, constant-only initializers, and position-independent code.
takeaways: Global variables live in the data section (initialized) or BSS/common (uninitialized), not on the stack.
Globals are added to the variable map under their assembly label, and that entry must persist across top-level items.
Uninitialized globals are zero-filled; BSS stores only their size to keep binaries small.
Global initializers must be constants because values are set before the program starts.
Position-independent code avoids absolute addresses and is needed for shared libraries and ASLR.
summary.summary: This is part 10 of Nora Sandler's series on writing a C compiler for 32-bit x86. It adds global variables: the parser now handles a list of top-level function or variable declarations, and code generation places initialized globals in the .data section and uninitialized ones in BSS (Linux) or the common section (macOS). The post explains assembly directives for these sections, how to map globals to labels in the variable map, and which validation checks are needed. It also includes a side discussion of position-independent executables and ASLR.
